To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of calcifications within the axillary lymph nodes in the absence of any history of previous exposure should raise the possibility that the patient has tuberculosis.

(1) Breast cancer coexisting with tuberculosis in axillary lymph nodes has not been described previously; (2) Breast cancer coexistent with tuberculosis in axilla should be considered in the differential diagnosis of breast cancer in the presence of calcifications; (3) Tuberculosis involving axillary lymph nodes can create diagnostic dilemmas in the presence of malignant process; (4) The presence of calcification in lymph nodes should be considered tuberculosis even without a history of contact with tuberculosis; (5)
the presence of calcifications within axillary lymph nodes should raise suspicion of tuberculous lymphadenitis even in patients who had no contact history of tuberculosis.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of calcification in a tuberculous lymph node should not preclude a diagnosis of malignancy in the breast, and that a thorough search for a primary breast cancer should be made in such cases.
tuberculosis should always be considered in the differential diagnosis of axillary lymph node calcifications, even in the absence a history of contact with tuberculosis.
breast cancer can be associated with tuberculous lymph nodes, and the possibility of such an association should be kept in mind when evaluating patients with breast cancer and suspicious lymph nodes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the possibility of tuberculosis should not be overlooked in patients presenting with breast cancer.
the diagnosis of breast carcinoma is a challenge for the pathologist and the radiologist when the patient has a history of tuberculosis.

tuberculosis of axillary nodes should be considered as a differential diagnosis of lymph node calcifications in breast imaging, and that a biopsy of the lymph node is mandatory to exclude tuberculosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the possibility of tuberculosis should be considered when evaluating lymph node calcifications, even in the absence a history of exposure to tuberculosis.
the presence of microcalcifications in axillary lymph nodes should prompt further investigations and consideration of tuberculosis.
breast cancer associated with tuberculous lymph nodes is rare, and it should always be considered when a patient presents with breast cancer associated with axillary lymphadenopathy.
